calls.result:
[user] A procurement catalog lists desk accessories and lighting products for employee workstations.
[user] Office buyers compare task lamps by brightness, adjustability, energy use, warranty, and price.
[user] Facilities teams select adjustable desk lamps for focused work and review product certifications before purchase.
[user] The Harbor Task Lamp is a standard desk lamp used in offices. The catalog describes it as adjustable and suitable for focused desk work.

output:
Short answer
- Aim for an ENERGY STAR / DLC-listed LED task lamp with dimming, an adjustable arm/head, good glare control and CRI ≥ 80. From your catalog memory, the Harbor Task Lamp is a candidate (it’s listed as adjustable and suitable for focused desk work) — but you must verify whether the Harbor model is an LED lamp and whether it carries energy-efficiency certifications before selecting it for an “energy-efficient” upgrade.

What I used from your catalog
- Memory entry: “Harbor Task Lamp is a standard desk lamp used in offices. The catalog describes it as adjustable and suitable for focused desk work.” Evidence available: adjustable and suitable for focused work (catalog statement).
- Missing from the catalog entry: lamp light source (LED vs halogen/incandescent), wattage, lumens, energy-efficiency certification (ENERGY STAR/DLC), dimming capability, color temperature, warranty, and price.

Recommended specification checklist (why each matters)
- LED integrated light source (or LED lamp/bulb): LEDs give highest lm/W (energy per light output). Evidence: industry-wide efficiency advantage of LEDs over incandescent/halogen/fluorescent. Claim to verify: whether the Harbor lamp is LED.
- ENERGY STAR or DLC listing: ensures efficiency and performance standards. Evidence: ENERGY STAR / DLC are standard third-party programs. Claim to verify: listing for any specific model.
- Lumens and efficacy: choose a lamp delivering ~450–800 lumens for task lighting and efficacy ≥ 80 lm/W. Why: gives sufficient task brightness while using less energy. Verify: catalog spec sheet for lm and W.
- Dimmable driver: saves energy when full brightness isn’t needed and improves user comfort. Verify: dimming range and control type.
- Color temperature ~3500–4000 K and CRI ≥ 80: neutral white and good color rendering for office tasks. Verify: CCT and CRI values.
- Adjustable arm/head with good ergonomics and glare control: ensures light is directed to task and reduces need for higher output. Catalog already supports adjustability for Harbor; verify extent of adjustability and shielding.
- Long warranty (3–5+ years) and replaceable LED module/drivers: reduces lifecycle costs and waste. Verify warranty terms.
- Low standby power / occupancy sensor (optional): further reduces energy use if desks are unoccupied frequently. Verify presence and standby power draw.

What to verify for the Harbor Task Lamp (catalog claim vs. required evidence)
- Claim in catalog: “adjustable and suitable for focused desk work.” Evidence: catalog text supports this — no further verification needed for adjustability claim itself.
- Claims requiring verification before procurement:
  - Is the Harbor model LED (integrated or uses LED bulbs) or an older technology? (Required)
  - What is the nominal wattage (W) and lumen output (lm)? (Required)
  - Does it have ENERGY STAR or DLC certification? (Required)
  - Is it dimmable and what dimming method is used? (Required if you plan to use dimming)
  - Color temperature (CCT) and CRI values. (Required)
  - Warranty length and whether LED modules/drivers are replaceable. (Required)
  - Price and total cost of ownership (purchase + maintenance + energy). (Required)
  - Any third-party test data (flicker, photometrics) if staff are sensitive to flicker/glare. (Recommended)

Suggested procurement steps
1. Request the spec sheet / cut sheet for the Harbor Task Lamp model(s) in the catalog.
2. Confirm (and document) LED vs non-LED, watts, lumens, lm/W, CCT, CRI, dimming, and certifications (ENERGY STAR/DLC).
3. If the Harbor lamp is not LED or lacks certifications, seek an ENERGY STAR-certified LED task lamp alternative with the checklist features above.
4. Get price, warranty, and replacement-part info; request a sample or pilot small set of lamps for staff feedback (light quality, adjustability, glare).
5. Use meter testing on a sample unit to confirm actual power draw and light distribution before large deployment.

Simple energy-savings example (illustrative — verify with local data)
- If an older 60 W desk lamp is replaced by a 10 W LED delivering similar task light:
  - Power saved per lamp = 50 W.
  - If used 2,000 hours/year → 50 W × 2,000 h = 100,000 Wh = 100 kWh/year.
  - At $0.15/kWh, savings ≈ $15/year per lamp.
- Note: this is illustrative; actual savings depend on the original lamp type, hours of use, local electricity cost, and the Harbor lamp’s actual wattage — all must be verified.

Bottom line recommendation
- Don’t buy purely on the Harbor listing alone. The Harbor Task Lamp’s adjustability makes it a plausible candidate, but verify that it’s an LED model with ENERGY STAR/DLC certification, adequate lumens, dimming, and warranty. If it lacks those, select a catalog alternative that meets the LED + certification + ergonomic checklist above.

If you want, I can:
- Draft an email/spec request to the vendor to obtain the Harbor lamp spec sheet (wattage, lumens, certs, warranty).
- Run a short cost-of-ownership calculator for a given lamp if you provide price, wattage, and expected hours/kWh rate.
